what:
User communication directive 2026-04-27 (extends #346 — no preemptive hype): when explaining UX flows / hook output / cross-editor parity, use **plain language about what the user sees and what the agent sees**, not technical jargon I invent (e.g. "chrome line," "chrome prefix," "audience-mapping," "audience split"). The user pushed back: "your table doesnt make sense, chrome line chrome prefix idk what you are saying ... explain tldr intended behavior we should have !!"

**Concrete rule for explaining hook/UX behavior:**
- Lead with the two surfaces the user actually cares about: (a) **what shows up in the chat** (user reads this), (b) **what the agent receives** (agent acts on this; user doesn't see).
- Don't introduce jargon ("chrome", "audience split", "render channel") in user-facing explanations even if it's correct in code comments.
- For each scenario (hard block, soft nudge, stop reminder, correction), explicitly say:
  - "User sees: <plain text or 'nothing'>"
  - "Agent sees: <plain text>"
- If the same content goes to both surfaces, say so directly. If only one surface receives content, say "user sees nothing" / "agent sees nothing" — don't dance around it.

**Where jargon IS fine:** code comments, internal memory entries (like #359 which uses the technical terms), commit messages. NOT in user-facing chat responses or external docs (cursor.md etc.).

**Pattern to remember:** if the user asks "TLDR" or "explain in plain words," that's a signal I've been over-jargonized previously and need to recalibrate the level. Don't just shorten — actually translate the technical concepts into observable user/agent behaviors.
why: User direct quote 2026-04-27: "your table doesnt make sense, chrome line chrome prefix idk what you are saying — explain tldr intended behavior we should have !!" I had been using internal-jargon terms (chrome, audience-mapping, render channel) in user-facing explanations. The user wants plain "what user sees / what agent sees" framing. Storing as priority:always so future cross-editor / UX explanations default to plain-language framing rather than re-introducing the jargon.
